title: Arkansas Department of Health urges public to recognize stroke signs on World Stroke Day
text:
Arkansas Department of Health urges public to recognize stroke signs on World Stroke Day
The Arkansas Department of Health is urging residents to recognize stroke symptoms and act quickly on World Stroke Day. The state continues efforts to improve stroke care access and outcomes, emphasizing the importance of immediate medical attention.
In recognition of World Stroke Day on October 29, the Arkansas Department of Health is urging residents to learn the warning signs of stroke and call 911 immediately if they occur. Stroke remains a significant health concern in Arkansas, with 1,971 Arkansans dying from stroke in 2024, giving the state one of the highest stroke death rates in the nation.
"Recognizing the signs of stroke and getting medical care quickly can save lives and reduce the risk of long-term disability. Many strokes can be prevented. Managing blood pressure, staying active, choosing healthier foods, and quitting smoking can all help reduce your risk," Bala Simon, MD, DrPH, Deputy Chief Medical Officer and State Chronic Disease Director, said, according to the Arkansas Department of Health.
Stroke is described as a medical emergency that occurs when blood flow to the brain is blocked, causing long-term damage with every minute treatment is delayed. Patients who arrive at the hospital within three hours of their first symptoms often experience less disability months later compared to those who receive delayed care. The department encourages Arkansans to remember the acronym BE FAST to recognize the warning signs: sudden loss of balance or coordination, sudden vision changes, face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty, and the importance of calling 911 immediately. Any one of these symptoms could be a sign of stroke, and immediate action is urged even if symptoms go away.
Arkansas is working to improve access to timely stroke care across the state. The Arkansas Stroke Ready Hospital designation program recognizes hospitals that meet state requirements to ensure patients experiencing stroke receive appropriate care as quickly as possible. Currently, 46 hospitals in Arkansas have a stroke designation or certification through the Arkansas Department of Health or a national accrediting organization. Additional hospitals participate in telestroke programs, expanding access to specialized stroke care.
Hospitals seeking Stroke Ready designation work with the department to demonstrate they have the staff, protocols, and training needed to rapidly evaluate, treat, and, when necessary, transfer patients experiencing stroke. Data from the Arkansas Stroke Registry shows continued improvement in the timeliness and quality of stroke care. The percentage of eligible stroke patients who received all recommended care increased from 62% in 2019 to 79% in 2025, according to the Arkansas Stroke Registry.
The department continues to strengthen coordination between emergency medical services and hospitals and expand access to specialized stroke care through statewide telestroke partnerships. These efforts are designed to help patients receive the right care as quickly as possible, regardless of where they live. On World Stroke Day, the Arkansas Department of Health encourages every Arkansan to remember one simple message: BE FAST.
